details:
**Jean-Jacques Rousseau's The Social Contract (1762)**
Rousseau's treatise, full title The Social Contract, or Principles of Political Right (Du contrat social). It argues that the only legitimate political authority comes from an agreement in which each person joins a collective body. It is the most common giveaway for this answer.

**"Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains"**
The famous opening line of Rousseau's The Social Contract. It introduces his question of how political authority over naturally free people can be made legitimate.

**General will and the sovereign**
In Rousseau's theory, the whole body of citizens forms "the sovereign," which acts through the general will, meaning the common good of all rather than the sum of private interests. Laws that the people have not approved are null and void, and the sovereign cannot alienate (give away) the general will. Anyone who refuses to obey the general will may be "forced to be free."

**Veil of ignorance and the original position**
John Rawls's thought experiment in A Theory of Justice (1971). In the "original position," people choose the principles of justice from behind a "veil of ignorance" that hides their own race, class, talents, and other personal details, so they cannot choose rules that favor themselves. It is Rawls's modern version of the social contract.

**State of nature and the "war of all against all" (Leviathan)**
In Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan (1651), life in the state of nature, before government, is a "war of all against all" in which life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short." People escape it by making a contract that gives power to an absolute sovereign.

**John Locke's Second Treatise of Government and the right of revolution**
Locke argued that people leave the state of nature by consent, explicit or tacit, to form a government that protects their natural rights to life, liberty, and property. If the government breaks this trust, the people may rebel and form a new government.

**Critique of Hugo Grotius and "force does not create right"**
Early chapters of Rousseau's Social Contract attack Grotius's defense of slavery. Rousseau defines "alienate" as "to give or sell" and argues that no one can give up all his liberty. He says that force does not create right, because slaves obey out of fear of harm, not out of moral obligation.

**Hot climates and population growth**
Book III of Rousseau's Social Contract says that hot climates suit despotism or monarchy. Because moral qualities cannot be measured, he says population growth is the "surest mark" of a good government. The same section discusses the Roman comitia (popular assemblies) and Caligula's claim to be a god.

**Death penalty as a "gift made conditionally"**
Rousseau defended capital punishment in The Social Contract. He argued that a citizen's life is no longer just a gift of nature but "a gift made conditionally by the State," so a criminal who breaks the contract can lose it.

**David Hume's critique ("Of the Original Contract")**
In his essay "Of the Original Contract," Hume argued that real governments were almost never founded on consent. Instead, they began through conquest or usurpation and draw their authority from habit and tradition.

**Plato's Crito**
An ancient forerunner of social contract thinking. In the Crito, Socrates refuses to escape from prison before his execution, because by living in Athens he had implicitly agreed to obey its laws.

**David Gauthier's Morals by Agreement (1986)**
A contractarian work in which Gauthier argues that morality arises from rational bargaining between self-interested agents. Agents do best by being "constrained maximizers," meaning they cooperate with others who are also willing to cooperate.

**Charles Mills's The Racial Contract (1997)**
Mills argues that the real social contract of modern Western political thought was a "racial contract" among white people. In his view, this contract excluded non-white people and upheld white supremacy.

**Kant and Perpetual Peace**
Immanuel Kant treated the original contract as an "idea of reason," a test of a law's legitimacy rather than a historical event. In Perpetual Peace he applied contract-style reasoning between states and proposed a federation of free states to end war.
